title: Eight wines under £10 that offer amazing value, from The Wine Society
summary: It’s getting very hard to find wines that retail under £10 in the UK and which still have any character,
content:
It’s getting very hard to find wines that retail under £10 in the UK and which still have any character, because of the recent increase in taxation. But The Wine Society seem to have a gift for sniffing out bargains, and I have pulled out a few gems here from yesterday’s excellent press tasting.

Lou Blanc Pacherenc du Vic-Bilh 2022 France
14% alcohol. This is made by Plaimont and it’s a blend of Gros Manseng, Petit Manseng and Petit Courbu, stainless steel fermented and aged. Weighty and delicious, this is layered with honeyed citrus and pear fruit. The fruit has a sweetness to it (although it’s a dry wine), and everything is nicely hemmed in by spicy acidity. 92/100 (£9.95 The Wine Society)

Emiliana Silbador Gewurztraminer 2025 Rapel, Chile
13% alcohol. Made by organic specialists Emiliana. This is a beautiful Gewurztraminer with rose petal, pear and lychee notes. It’s not too showy, and comes across as fresh and pure with nice depth. Dry. 91/100 (£8.95 The Wine Society)

Domaine Emile Boeckel Alsace Blanc 2025 France
12.5% alcohol. A blend of Sylvaner, Muscat and Pinot Blanc. This is beautifully expressive with some grapey, lychee prettiness and also notes of honey, peach and pear. Delicious stuff with just a hint of sweetness (rs 6.2 g/litre). Impressive for the price. 90/100 (£9.95 The Wine Society)

Château Beaubois Un Amour de Cinsault 2025 France
11.5% alcohol. From the Costières de Nîmes this is a biodynamic Cinsault of real class. Fresh raspberry and cherry fruit nose with some wild herbs. Very Cinsault in character. The palate is pure and focused with nice balance to the fresh red cherry and plum fruit. 92/100 (£9.95 The Wine Society)

Feudo Arancio Nero d’Avola 2024 Sicily, Italy
13% alcohol. This carries 6.3 g/l residual sugar, but I didn’t spot it. There’s lovely fruit purity with cherries, raspberries and a lick of spice and pepper. Nice weight: this is just about the pure fruit. 90/100 (£9.25 The Wine Society)

The Society’s Barbera d’Asti Superiore 2023 Piemonte, Italy
13% alcohol. I was really impressed by this own-label Barbera. Lovely weight and balance here with nice density and a wet stone edge to the pure cherry and plum fruit. Good concentration and superb balance. 91/100 (£9.95 The Wine Society)

AA Badenhorst Fontein Cabernet Sauvignon Syrah 2026 Swartland, South Africa
13.5% alcohol. A lovely fresh, drinkable baby wine (this is 2026!). Fresh, floral, expressive nose is juicy and bright with nice grip, as well as supple, open cherry and strawberry fruit. Delicious with lovely drinkability and a bit of grip on the finish. 91/100 (£9.95 The Wine Society)

Undurraga Candelabro Carmenere 2025 Maule, Chile
14% alcohol. This is brilliant. Fresh, floral blackcurrant fruit with some cherry and spice. Nice freshness on the palate with some structure, showing lovely vivid, sweet fruit and nice brightness. 92/100 (£9.95 The Wine Society)

title: Visiting Montes, a major Chilean winery who are making the switch to regenerative viticulture
summary: I visited Montes with Rodrigo Barral chief viticulturist and Santiago Izcúe, winemaker. It was an interesting visit: this is a
content:
I visited Montes with Rodrigo Barral chief viticulturist and Santiago Izcúe, winemaker. It was an interesting visit: this is a rather special vineyard, with the main part of the property consisting of an amphitheatre-like arrangement of vines on hillsides at the end of the Apalta Valley in Colchagua. It’s varied and quite beautiful.

Montes has 120 hectares of vines here in Apalta, plus another 450 in Marchigüe, also in Colchagua but closer to the ocean, so a cooler site. They also have the 47 hectare Zapallar vineyard in coastal Acongcagua. The project dates back to the late 1980s, when it was founded by Aurelio Montes and a couple of partners, and has grown significantly since then.

Four years ago, Aurelio Montes asked Rodrigo to look at converting the vineyards to organics. But Rodrigo says that this didn’t sit well with him. The motivation for this was that they were becoming concerned about the resilience of the vineyard. A look at the chart plotting GDDs over the last 24 years showed that there was a slow rise, but from 2015 the seasons have varied a lot, with a big fluctuation of el niño and el niña years. In terms of GDDs the cooler seasons are below 1600, and the warmer ones past 1800, and with these fluctuations there’s quite a variation in rainfall. Climate chaos is the new normal!

Rodrigo had been to a seminar on climate change and regenerative farming, and decided that rather than heading down the organic path, a switch to regenerative would be the best route to take, because it promises to increase the resilience of the vineyard. So this is what they have done.

Vermicasting is an interesting process. Unlike normal warm composting, it’s a cold process that doesn’t generate a lot of heat. It is usually done with a species of worm called Eisenia fetida, also known as the red wriggler, and it’s a surface dwelling epigeic worm well suited to this task.

They produce vermicast using the Biofiltro system that I’ve written about before. This is a 30 x 40 metre plot where they use wood chips and cardboard waste, and water it with minimally treated winery waste water. The worms break down the wood and cardboard, cleaning the waste water in the process, and this is of the quality to be used for irrigation. And a by-product is the black gold: vermicast.

Another thing they do is to make JADAM compost tea. This is a cheap and effective way of culturing microorganisms that you can then add back to the soil.

For composting, they use wool and grape marc, and mix in some vermicast. They control the temperature because they want lots of fungus, and if the temperature gets too high the fungus is lost. 500 m3 ends up as 250 m3 at the end of the process. They use it at a concentration of 4 tonnes/hectare in new blocks and any weaker blocks.

They are still learning about cover cropping and managing them in this site. They use a roller crimper to terminate the cover crop as the vines get going, and a finger weeder for undervine.  ‘The weeds were our enemies,’ says Rodrigo, ‘but now they help us to have the natural balance in the whole vineyard.’

They have been measuring fungi, bacteria and protozoa in the soils from 2023. The new farming regime has had measurable impact. Potassium increased 31% and phosphorus 22%, so they no longer have to add these as inputs. Overall, they have reduced inputs in Apalta by 31%, and in Marchigüe they are down 54%. They no longer use any herbicides in Apalta, and they’ve reduced herbicide use in the much larger Marchigüe vineyard by 49%.

One of the goals of regenerative farming is increasing soil organic material. This also has a side-benefit of reducing atmospheric carbon dioxide. Rodrigo showed me some data. In first 30 cm of soil, if you increase organic matter by 1% this stores 83 tonnes of CO2 per hectare. If we do this in all agricultural soils in the world, he points out, then we’ll be storing 130 gigatons, mitigating 7 years of CO2 rises. When they started the regenerative program, their soil organic material was 1.5% and three years later it is 3%. Adding +0.4% organic material per year offsets all their carbon dioxide emissions.

THE WINES

Outer Limits Albariño 2025 Zapallar, Aconcagua
This is 7 km from the Ocean and has a strong cooling influence, and it works well for Albariño. Natural decantation, 80 NTUs so the juice is very clean, 14 C fermentation temperature in stainless steel. This is pure, vivid and quite primary with crisp, clean citrus fruit and some pear drop esters from the fermentation still. Fresh and crystalline with a touch or apricot. 90/100

Outer Limits Sauvignon Blanc 2024 Zapallar, Aconcagua
12 h cold maceration, natural decanting, long fermentation at low temperature. Bottle young. Chalky and a bit green on the nose. Vivid citrussy fruit with a touch of elderflower. Good concentration with well-integrated green notes and good acidity, and a nice chalky edge. 88/100

Outer Limits Pinot Noir 2023 Zapallar, Acongcagua
One tank is carbonic (100%, pressed and finished fermentation in liquid phase), second tank is destemmed, third is stems added back in layers. This makes three different wines. This is silky and fruity with nice complexity: there’s sweet cherry fruit but also hints of undergrowth and spice. It’s warm and spicy, but also fresh and quite layered. A lovely Pinot Noir. 93/100

Outer Limits CGM 2024 Apalta, Colchagua
Carigan, Grenache and Mourvèdre from Apalta. Use gravity instead of pumps. They use commercial yeasts. Stainless steel for fermentation, 3 pump overs a day (short and gentle), short macerations. Rack into concrete eggs and old barrels, in order to get some softness. This is juicy and energetic with vivid black cherry and blackberry fruit with some firm, grippy tannins and good acidity. Juicy and linear with a touch of pepper on the finish. 93/100

Montes Alpha Cabernet Sauvignon 2015 Colchagua
15% Merlot in the blend. 50% new French oak. This has a powerful nose of mint and blackcurrant with a hint of vinyl and tar. Intriguing. The palate is still youthful with some dusty blackcurrant fruit and good structure, as well as bright acidity. Very minty! Nice balance here with a remarkable personality, and still with potential for further development. 93/100

Purple Angel by Montes Carmenère 2021 Colchagua
92% Carmenère, 8% Petit Verdot. Aged in French oak, 70% new. This is benchmark Carmenère with ripe blackcurrant fruit, some chalkiness, and then black cherries, some mulchy leafy characters, fig and pepper, with some grippy tannin. There’s a lovely density and intensity to this wine, with black fruits to the fore and a hint of blackberry jam. This has a lot of personality, and the oak is just swallowed up by the fruit, with a nice mouthfeel. 94/100

title: Arnaldo Rivera, a top tier of wines from the overperforming Terre del Barolo cooperative
summary: Websites: https://terredelbarolo.com/en/  https://arnaldorivera.com/en/ The Terre del Barolo cooperative was founded in 1958 in Castiglione. First vintage was 1959, and today
content:
Websites: https://terredelbarolo.com/en/  https://arnaldorivera.com/en/

The Terre del Barolo cooperative was founded in 1958 in Castiglione. First vintage was 1959, and today they are an important player in the region. In 2017 they began the Arnaldo Rivera project, named after the founder of the cooperative. I met with Gabriele Oderda, Director of Arnaldo Rivera, on a video call, to chat through this interesting project while tasting five wines.

Gabriele emphasized that understanding Arnoldo Rivera today requires an understanding of how Barolo has developed as a region. These days, it’s famous and the top wines are expensive, but this wasn’t always the case.

After the second world war, Langhe was one of poorest agricultural areas of all northern Italy. This isn’t all that long ago. It was in 1958 that Arnaldo Rivera began the cooperative Terre del Barolo. He was an important figure in the region and for 37 years was mayor of Castiglione Faletto. ‘He was a man of the people, the guy that you want to call for an advice,’ says Gabriele. ‘This was the time when Giacomo Oddero was mayor in La Mora, Battista Rinaldi was mayor in Barolo and Giovanni Gaja was mayor in Barbaresco. It was an all-star game. These are the founding fathers of the modern Barolo. And also Arnaldo Rivera during his lifetime was one of the closest friends of Bartolo Mascarello himself. But he did something different from all these people. He didn’t put his own family name on the label. But he put the community ahead. And he thought of building a winery for the people.’

One of the motivations for forming the cooperative was because of how badly the growers were being treated in the grape market of Alba. ‘It was known locally as the dead people market, because of the depreciation in the price of the grapes,’ says Gabriele. ‘The grape market was ruled by just a few brokers.’

What happened in Barolo opened the path for quality, says Gabriele. In contrast, things didn’t work out so well in the north of Piemonte. At the beginning of the 20th century this northern part of the region was one of the most intensively planted regions in Italy, but a lot of the vineyards have now gone. Workers left from the vineyards to the textile industry and to the cities. This could have happened to the Langhe, too, but it didn’t.

Terre del Barolo is the only grower cooperative in Barolo. When Analdo Rivera founded it, only 22 growers joined the first year. The next year, 250 joined. ‘We are a little bit like the sheep in Italy, we never move,’ says Gabriele. ‘We look around, but we don’t move. If one starts to go, everyone follows. So, as soon as they started to build a winery, in the springtime of 1959, there was a big attraction towards the coop.’

Arnaldo Rivera stipulated some conditions for those who wanted to join. They needed to be located in one of the 11 villages of Barolo, they needed to own their vineyards, and all their grapes had to come to the cooperative. And the grapes needed to come to the cooperative in small boxes, with no pressing at the farm. This allows the strict control of quality.

The cooperative is significant for the region, making 12% of all Barolo. The whole appellation is 2200 hectares, and cooperative members have 240 of these.

Terre del Barolo have a number of tiers of quality, in a sort of pyramid. At the bottom is bulk wine, sold to supermarkets and big players, enabling them to get quality at a good price. Then there’s middle range, which is the core of their production. And the top tier is around 10% of production, and this is Arnoldo Rivera, which is a completely separate philosophy, based on vineyard-designated wines. 35 of the 300 growers Terre del Barolo contribute to this tier. They are paid according to the potential yield of their site, so it is about enabling them to farm well, with a specific vineyard protocol. ‘This Arnaldo Rivera philosophy was born from the bottom,’ says Gabriele. ‘This is not a director’s marketing programme.’

As well as Barolo, they have added some interesting grape varieties to the range, including Freisa, Verduno Pelaverga, Dolcetto and Nascetta (a rare white variety).

I asked Gabriele about where the cooperative sat on the modernist/traditionalist Barolo discussions of the past. ‘Our winery is a farmer cooperatives. And when we think about taking a decision with the 300 heads, this is very time consuming. Sometimes being slow provides luck!’ So they didn’t jump on the modernist small-oak bandwagon. ‘We passed the trend. We didn’t even notice.’ They stuck with the large-format wooden casks. But when they stared started Arnoldo Rivera ten years ago they had to buy some smaller vessels because they were dealing with small plot vinifications. ‘We have Rocche Castiglione, which is a vineyard of 0.34 hectares. We cannot fill a large cask.’ For smaller oak, they are very careful about the barrels, they test the staves and everything is not toasted, but staves are bent by vapour and not fire to limit the impact on the wine.

Arnaldo Rivera Langhe Nascetta del Commune di Novello 2024 Piemonte, Italy
13% alcohol. Nascetta is a rare variety that’s unique to the commune of Novello in Barolo. No oak here, but an extra year in bottle to help subdue some of the more floral terpenic notes. This is textured and quite broad with a subtly spicy edge to the rich pear and white peach fruit. It’s a really classy, full-flavoured wine, but has balance. Subtle notes of wax and toast, and some aniseed and sour cherry on the finish. Bold and quite delicious. 93/100

Arnaldo Rivera Undicicomuni Barolo 2022 Piemonte, Italy
14.5% alcohol. Potentially from all 11 communes in Barolo (they are the only producer to have grapes from all of them, but it wasn’t until 2025 that all made it into the blend), two years in large oak. This is rich, ripe and textured with some warm spiciness and nice structure under the red cherry and cranberry fruit, and there’s also a floral dimension on the nose. There’s some richness here, but it isn’t a heavy wine. The alcohol makes its presence felt, and the fruit sweetness coats the tannins. Finishes warm and spicy. There’s a harmonious integration to this wine. This is a classic Barolo from a warm vintage that should age in interesting ways: it picks up some weight and structure on day 2 after opening. 94/100

Arnaldo Rivera Barolo Ravera 2022 Piemonte, Italy
14.5% alcohol. From five sites in this south-facing MGA. 30 months in cask. Just 4500 bottles made. Lovely aromatics with warm spices, some cedar hints, rose petal, iodine, wild strawberry and red cherry. The palate shows raspberry, cherry and strawberry with lovely texture and a hint of mint and pot pourri. This is a lovely wine with ripeness, detail, structure but also elegance. Some alcoholic warmth. 94/100

Arnaldo Rivera Barolo Bussia 2022 Piemonte, Italy
15% alcohol. From two sites facing southwest in this MGA. 30 months in cask, 3600 bottes. Lovely pale cherry red in colour. Some warmth on the nose, with red cherries and redcurrants as well as fine spicy notes. Elegant despite the alcohol, with dried herbs and some rose petal. The palate is textured, warm, elegant and has some smoothness from the high alcohol. There’s a real harmony and delicacy here, as well as ripe fruit and some alcoholic warmth. Lovely stuff and should age really well. 95/100

Arnaldo Rivera Verduno Pelaverga Suicristalli 2025 Piemonte, Italy
13.5% alcohol. Lighter red in colour. Wonderful aromatics of sweet cherry and aniseed with some leafy green notes and black pepper. The palate has lovely texture and detail, with a bit of structure and good acidity. Such a distinctive variety showing its best here. Massive drinkability, but also a bit of seriousness. I love it. 94/100
